Question three. What is an index, and when does it help, or hurt? It's a sorted structure over a column, a B-tree by default, where each value points at its rows. It helps when a filter is selective. Postgres finds forty-two in the index, then reads only the twenty pages that hold its rows, out of seven thousand three hundred sixty. It doesn't help when most rows match. Nine in ten orders are shipped, so even with an index on status, Postgres scans the table: one pass beats nine hundred thousand jumps. And every index costs writes. Ten thousand inserted rows wrote ten thousand log records with no index, and four times that with three.

Question four. What is a covering index? One that holds every column a query needs, so the table itself is never read. This query wants customer ID and amount. Add amount to the index with include, and the plan becomes an index only scan, with zero heap fetches. The price is size: this index is four times the plain one, and every insert writes all of it. Cover the few queries that run constantly.

Question five. What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index? A clustered index sets the order rows are stored in, so a table gets one. A non-clustered index is a separate lookup, and you can have many. Postgres has no clustered index. Its cluster command sorts the table by an index once. Customer forty-two's twenty orders sat on twenty pages; after cluster, they share one. But the order isn't kept: the next order for forty-two lands on the table's last page.
